drafts.speaker: Reem
drafts.script:
Part One

When our school introduced a competition for practical inventions, I joined a team of four students who wanted to reduce wasted electricity in the library. The lights often remained on in empty study areas. Our first idea was a motion sensor, but before building anything, we watched how visitors used the room at different times of day. We discovered that quiet readers sometimes sat almost completely still for an hour. A sensor that switched off the lights whenever nobody moved would make reading difficult.

Our physics teacher suggested testing a combination of movement and a manual timer. We borrowed a small controller and measured how long it took to detect movement. During the first trial, the lights went off while two students were revising. We asked them what had happened, then changed the system so that a desk could remain lit for twenty minutes after the last movement. A clearly marked button also allowed readers to extend the time.

Part Two

The next challenge was cost. Our design needed more components than we had expected. We prepared a simple price list and chose to reuse a safe working sensor from another school project. An electrician checked the wiring before anyone connected the device to the lighting demonstration board. No pupil was allowed to work directly with the building's electrical supply.

On presentation day, we invited the librarian to test the demonstration. She liked the timer, but pointed out that the button was difficult to reach for someone sitting in a wheelchair. We moved the control to the front of the desk and asked another volunteer to try it.

Our invention did not immediately save electricity across the whole library. It was a small model that helped us test an idea responsibly. The most useful lesson was that a clever design must consider the people who will use it, not just the technology inside it.

drafts.speaker: Khalid
drafts.script:
Part One

Last winter, I volunteered at a transport information desk during a weekend festival near the coast. Hundreds of visitors arrived by bus, car and taxi, and many were unfamiliar with the area. My job was to help them find the correct departure point for their return journey. I was given a printed map of the temporary bus stops and a list of departure times, but I quickly learned that a map alone was not enough.

On Saturday morning, a family asked how to reach the railway exhibition. The nearest shuttle bus stopped beside the old market, a ten-minute walk from our desk. I explained the route and showed them the accessible entrance. Later, a visitor told me that the route on one sign was confusing because two streets had similar names. I walked with a supervisor to check the sign rather than guessing.

Part Two

At lunchtime, the organisers announced that part of the waterfront road would close for a cycling event. The shuttle could no longer use its usual stop. The transport team moved it to the northern car park and posted the change on the festival website. We also placed a temporary notice at the original stop and asked volunteers to guide passengers to the new location. Some visitors had already printed the earlier timetable, so we explained the change in person.

That afternoon, a passenger using a wheelchair asked whether the replacement stop had a safe ramp. I did not know the answer. I contacted the transport supervisor, who confirmed that an accessible vehicle would collect passengers at a marked waiting area. This took several minutes, but giving a verified answer mattered more than sounding confident.

By the end of the festival, I understood how quickly travel arrangements can change. Clear signs, accurate departure times and patient communication helped visitors reach their destinations. I also learned that saying 'I will check' is sometimes the most responsible response.
